title: The poem, its title and date
short: A lament for dead poets ('makaris') printed by Chepman and Myllar in Edinburgh, 1508; usually dated c. 1505.
body: Dunbar's poem was first printed by Walter Chepman and Androw Myllar in Edinburgh in 1508, among the earliest Scottish printed books; the manuscript copies are later. Internal evidence (Walter Kennedy is still alive, but near death) points to about 1505. 'Makar' is the Scots word for a poet, a maker, exactly translating Greek 'poietes'. The opening is personal: 'I that in heill [health] was and gladness / Am trublit now with great sickness / And feblit [enfeebled] with infirmitie'. Whether Dunbar was really ill or adopting a conventional sick-bed persona is uncertain. The poem is a 'danse macabre' (dance of death) that narrows from all estates of society to Dunbar's fellow poets and finally to himself.

title: Timor mortis conturbat me
greek: Latin: 'the fear of death disturbs me'
short: A Latin refrain from a responsory in Matins of the Office of the Dead: 'the fear of death troubles me'.
body: The refrain comes from the liturgy for the dead: in the third nocturn of Matins in the Office of the Dead, the responsory 'Peccantem me quotidie' confesses daily sin without repentance and continues 'timor mortis conturbat me', because in hell there is no redemption. A late medieval reader would know the words from funerals and from the prayers of the Book of Hours. The phrase was a popular refrain in English and Scots poetry; the archive's anonymous Middle English 'In what state that ever I be' uses it too. Repeated after every stanza, it works like a tolling bell and a penitential response, and the fear it names is spiritual as well as physical.

title: bruckle; slee
short: 'Bruckle' is brittle, frail; 'slee' is sly, cunning: the old triad of world, flesh and devil.
body: 'Bruckle' (brittle, fragile, easily broken) is a Scots word Dunbar often uses for human life; 'the Feynd' is the devil, and 'slee' (sly) means crafty. With 'This fals world' in the previous line the stanza names the three traditional enemies of the soul, the world, the flesh and the devil, as in the Litany's prayer for deliverance 'from all the deceits of the world, the flesh, and the devil'. 'Vain glory' recalls Ecclesiastes 1:2 ('vanity of vanities'). The stanza sets the moral frame before the catalogue of the dead.

title: Mutability
short: The anaphora 'now ... now' presents life's sudden reversals; 'blyth' is happy, 'sary' sorry, 'dansand' dancing.
body: The third stanza turns the theme of mutability into rhythm: 'Now sound, now sick, now blyth, now sary, / Now dansand mirry, now like to die'. The repeated 'now' (anaphora) imitates the swing of Fortune's wheel, a medieval commonplace descending from Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy. 'Dansand' (dancing), with the Scots present participle in '-and', may hint at the dance of death, the pictorial and poetic tradition in which Death leads people of every rank away.

title: The wicker in the wind
short: 'Sicker' is secure; the world's vanity sways ('wannis', wanes) like a willow shoot in the wind.
body: 'No state in Erd here standis sicker' means no condition on earth stands secure ('sicker', from Latin 'securus'). The simile compares worldly vanity to the 'wicker', a pliant willow twig, that bends this way and that in the wind; 'wannis' (wanes) suggests diminishing as well as wavering. The image recalls biblical figures of human frailty as reeds and grass (e.g. Matthew 11:7, 'a reed shaken with the wind'). The alliteration of w-sounds ('wynd wavis ... wicker ... wannis ... world') imitates the movement.

title: All estates: the dance of death
short: Death takes all estates, princes, prelates and those in power, rich and poor: the roll-call of the danse macabre.
body: 'Estatis' are the orders or ranks of society. Dunbar lists princes, prelates (bishops and abbots) and 'Potestatis' (powers, rulers; compare the 'principalities' and 'powers' of Ephesians 6:12), then rich and poor of every degree. This is the logic of the danse macabre, familiar from murals and from Lydgate's English 'Dance of Death' (after the Paris Cemetery of the Innocents), where Death leads pope, emperor, knight, child and labourer in turn. The following stanzas personify Death as a conqueror taking knights, babies, champions, ladies, lords and clerks.

anchor: Victor he is at all mellie
title: mellie
short: 'Mellie' is a melee, a hand-to-hand fight: Death is victor in every battle; 'enarmit' means armed.
body: Death is imagined as a knight-champion who takes knights from the field 'Enarmit [armed] under helm and scheild' and is 'Victor ... at all mellie', winner in every melee or close combat (Scots 'melle', from Old French 'meslee'). The chivalric diction turns the personified Death into a superior warrior, against whom armour is useless, an idea echoed in stanza 8's 'campion in the stour'.

title: The babe at the breast
short: 'Tyrand' is tyrant; Death snatches even the infant 'sowkand' (sucking) at its mother's breast.
body: 'That strong unmerciful tyrand' (tyrant) is Death, who takes 'on the motheris breast sowkand [sucking], / The babe full of benignitie [innocence, goodness]'. The image is one of the most affecting in the dance-of-death tradition, where an infant is often shown being taken from its cradle. It sets Death's lack of mercy against the child's 'benignitie'. 'Sowkand' shows the Older Scots present participle ending in '-and'.

title: campion; stour; tour; bour
short: 'Campion' is a champion, 'stour' battle or tumult; the captain in his tower, the lady in her bower.
body: 'Campion' (champion, fighter) and 'stour' (conflict, battle, also dust and turmoil) are both Older Scots words of romance and chronicle. The stanza then sets the 'captain closit in the tour' (enclosed in the tower, defending a castle) against 'the lady in bour [bower] full of bewtie', so that strength, safety and beauty alike are powerless. The rhyme 'stour / tour / bour' links the three.

title: The learned professions
short: Magicians, astrologers, rhetoricians, logicians and theologians cannot argue their way out of death: 'conclusionis slee' are clever proofs.
body: Having shown that lords and clerks cannot escape ('piscence' is puissance, power; 'straik' a stroke), Dunbar lists the learned: practitioners of magic arts, astrologers, 'Rethoris' (rhetoricians), logicians and theologians. 'Them helpis no conclusionis slee': no subtle conclusions help them. 'Conclusions' were both syllogistic proofs and alchemical or astrological experiments. There is irony in a poet (himself a master of rhetoric) admitting that eloquence and learning cannot save anyone.

sources.cite: Dictionaries of the Scots Language (Dictionary of the Older Scottish Tongue)

anchor: Themself from Death may not supplee
title: Physicians
short: Leeches, surgeons and physicians cannot 'supplee' (succour, save) themselves: an echo of 'Physician, heal thyself' (Luke 4:23).
body: 'The most practicianis' are the most skilful practitioners of medicine; 'Leechis' are physicians (from Old English 'laece'), 'surrigianis' surgeons. They 'may not supplee' themselves, cannot rescue or supply aid to themselves (Scots 'suppley', from Latin 'supplere'). The idea recalls the proverb in Luke 4:23, 'Physician, heal thyself'. The stanza ends the list of the professions and prepares the turn to the poets.

title: The turn to the poets
short: 'The lave' is the rest: poets too play their 'padyanis' (pageants) and then go to the grave.
body: With stanza 12 the poem turns to its true subject. 'I see that makaris amang the lave [the rest] / Playis here their padyanis [pageants], syne [then] gois to grave': poets act out their part on the world's stage like players in a pageant, and their 'facultie' (art, gift) is not spared. The theatrical image (the world as a stage) was widespread in medieval and Renaissance moral writing. What follows is the first literary history of Scottish poetry, a roll-call of poets, many of whose works are lost.

anchor: The noble Chaucer, of makaris flour
title: Chaucer, the Monk of Bury, Gower
short: Chaucer (d. 1400), 'flower of poets'; the Monk of Bury is John Lydgate (d. c. 1451); John Gower (d. 1408).
body: Dunbar begins with the three English poets whom Scottish and English writers of the fifteenth century treated as their masters: Geoffrey Chaucer, 'of makaris flour' (the flower of poets); John Lydgate, monk of Bury St Edmunds; and John Gower. The triad was conventional, and Dunbar praises the same three in 'The Goldyn Targe'. 'He has done petuously devour' means Death has piteously devoured them. Opening with the English masters places the Scots poets that follow in a common tradition of 'makaris'.

title: Sir Hew of Eglintoun
short: Hugh of Eglinton (d. 1377), brother-in-law of Robert II; his identification with the poet 'Huchoun' is uncertain.
body: Sir Hugh of Eglinton was a fourteenth-century Ayrshire knight (d. 1377) married to a half-sister of Robert II. No poem certainly by him survives. Andrew of Wyntoun mentions a poet called 'Huchoun of the Awle Ryale' (of the royal hall), and since the nineteenth century some have identified Huchoun with Hugh of Eglinton and credited him with alliterative works such as the 'Morte Arthure' or 'The Awntyrs off Arthure'. These identifications are disputed and unproven. Dunbar's list proves only that Hugh was remembered as a poet a century later.

title: Ettrick, Heriot, Wintoun
short: Ettrick and Heriot are unidentified; Andrew of Wyntoun (d. c. 1425) wrote the verse 'Orygynale Cronykil of Scotland'.
body: Of the three names in this line only Wintoun can be identified: Andrew of Wyntoun, prior of St Serf's, Lochleven, whose 'Orygynale Cronykil of Scotland' is a verse chronicle from the creation to his own day. Nothing is known of Ettrick or Heriot as poets. 'He has tane out of this cuntrie' (taken from this country) closes the stanza. As with many names in the poem, Dunbar's list is our only evidence that these men wrote at all, which shows how much medieval Scots poetry has been lost.

title: Death as a scorpion
short: Death is a 'fell' (cruel) scorpion that 'infecks' (poisons); compare 'O death, where is thy sting?' (1 Corinthians 15:55).
body: Death becomes 'That scorpion fell' (that cruel scorpion), which 'has done infeck' (has infected, poisoned) Master John Clerk and James Afflek, taking them from 'ballat-making and tragedie'. The scorpion's sting recalls 1 Corinthians 15:55 ('O death, where is thy sting?') and the scorpions of Revelation 9:5. Neither Clerk nor Afflek can be identified with certainty (Afflek may be a James Auchinleck); 'ballat' means a poem or song, and 'tragedie' a serious narrative with an unhappy ending.

title: Holland and Barbour
short: Richard Holland wrote 'The Buke of the Howlat' (c. 1450); John Barbour (d. 1395) wrote 'The Bruce'.
body: Richard Holland was the author of 'The Buke of the Howlat' (Book of the Owl), an alliterative allegory of about 1450 written for the Douglas family. John Barbour, archdeacon of Aberdeen, wrote 'The Bruce' (c. 1375), the verse epic of Robert the Bruce and the Wars of Independence, the founding work of Scots literature. 'Berevit' means bereft, taken away. Sir Mungo Lockart of the Lee, whom Dunbar laments in the same stanza, has no known works and may be a knight who died in 1489.

title: Clerk of Tranent; Gilbert Hay
short: 'Anteris' are adventures; the Clerk of Tranent's Gawain romance is lost or unidentified. Sir Gilbert Hay translated and adapted prose and verse.
body: 'Anteris' (aventures, adventures) suggests an Arthurian romance about Gawain written by an unnamed 'Clerk of Tranent' (a village east of Edinburgh). Some have tried to link it to surviving alliterative romances such as 'The Awntyrs off Arthure', but this remains speculative. Sir Gilbert Hay (fl. 1456) is better known: he translated works on chivalry and government into Scots prose and is credited with 'The Buik of King Alexander the Conquerour'. 'Endit has he' means Death has ended him.

title: Blind Harry and the 'schour of mortal hail'
short: Blind Harry (d. c. 1492) wrote 'The Wallace'; Death kills with a 'shower of deadly hail'.
body: Blind Harry (Hary) was the author of 'The Wallace' (c. 1477), a long patriotic poem on William Wallace. Sandy Traill is unidentified. Death has 'slain with his schour of mortal hail' (shower of deadly hail), a battlefield image of arrows or missiles. 'Quhilk Patrick Johnstoun might nought flee' (which Patrick Johnstoun could not escape) is puzzling, since Johnstoun, a courtier with no surviving works, is thought to have been still alive when Dunbar wrote. 'Quh-' is the Scots spelling for 'wh-'.

title: Merseir
short: Death has robbed Mercer of his 'endite' (composition, writing); his love poems were brief, quick and 'of sentence hie' (lofty meaning).
body: 'Endite' is the act or art of composing. Mercer (Merseir) is praised for writing 'in luve so lively' (vividly), 'So short, so quick, of sentence hie' (of lofty sense), an unusually precise piece of literary criticism. A few love poems in the Bannatyne Manuscript are attributed to 'Mersar', perhaps the same man. The two Rowlls in the next stanza (of Aberdeen and of Corstorphine) are barely known; one poem survives attributed to a Roull.

title: Robert Henryson
short: Robert Henryson (d. c. 1500), schoolmaster at Dunfermline, author of 'The Testament of Cresseid' and the 'Morall Fabillis'.
body: The line 'In Dunfermline he has tane Broun / With Maister Robert Henrysoun' gives one of the few pieces of evidence for Henryson's death and his link with Dunfermline, where he was probably schoolmaster attached to the abbey. 'Maister' indicates a university master's degree. Henryson, author of 'The Testament of Cresseid' (a sequel to Chaucer's Troilus), the 'Morall Fabillis' and 'Orpheus and Eurydice', is now regarded with Dunbar as the greatest of the Older Scots makars. It is striking that Dunbar names him so briefly. Broun is unidentified.

title: Sir John the Ross; Stobo; Quintin Shaw
short: Sir John the Ross was Dunbar's second in 'The Flyting'; Quintin Shaw was Kennedy's; Stobo was the royal clerk John Reid.
body: Sir John Ross appears in 'The Flyting of Dunbar and Kennedie', the poetic insult contest, as Dunbar's 'commissar' (second); Quintin Shaw, named in the next stanza, served Kennedy in the same role, and one satire by him survives. 'Gentil Stobo' has been identified with John Reid, priest and notary who served as clerk under James II, III and IV. 'Enbrast' means embraced, a grim image of Death's hug. 'Last of a' (last of all) and 'wichtis' (people) are Scots forms.

title: Walter Kennedy
short: Kennedy (d. c. 1508), Dunbar's rival in 'The Flyting', is 'in point of death': still alive but dying. This dates the poem.
body: Walter Kennedy, a Carrick poet and graduate of Glasgow, was Dunbar's opponent in 'The Flyting', and author of 'The Passioun of Crist'. Here he is not yet dead but 'In point of Death lies verily', truly on the point of death; 'Great ruth it were' means it would be a great pity. Because Kennedy is thought to have died c. 1508, the stanza helps date the poem c. 1505-8. The affection shown to an old adversary suggests the Flyting was in part a literary game.

title: The poet's own turn
short: 'Brether' are brothers (fellow poets); 'of force I man' means 'by necessity I must'. Dunbar expects to be next.
body: The catalogue ends by turning on the speaker: 'Sen [since] he has all my brether tane [taken all my brothers], / He will naught let me live alane; / Of force [of necessity] I man [must] his next prey be'. 'Brether' expresses a fellowship of poets across Scotland and England. The poem thus returns to the sick 'I' of its opening, and the refrain's fear becomes personal. The ending of the list of makars with himself gives the poem its emotional force.

title: The last stanza
short: 'Remeid' is remedy; 'dispone' means prepare or dispose ourselves; so we may live after death.
body: The closing stanza turns from lament to counsel: since there is no 'remeid' (remedy) against death, it is best that we 'dispone' (prepare, set ourselves in order, from Latin 'disponere') for death, 'After our death that live may we', so that we may live in heaven after dying. This is the orthodox lesson of the art of dying ('ars moriendi'). Yet the poem still ends with the refrain 'Timor Mortis conturbat me', so that consolation and fear stand together. Critics differ on whether the final note is serene or still troubled.
